name: Three Federal Laws in Plain English
title: Three Federal Laws in Plain English
answer: Three federal laws carry most of the load when it comes to protecting students online: FERPA covers education records, COPPA covers the personal information of children under 13 on commercial sites and apps, and CIPA sets filtering and safety rules for schools that take federal internet discounts. A fourth law, the Protection of Pupil Rights Amendment, gives parents rights over surveys and marketing aimed at their children and can matter when an AI tool asks about sensitive topics. Knowing which law applies to which situation is the starting point for any school deciding how to use AI with students.

crumbs.name: Privacy, Safety, and the Human Review Rule

sections.body: This idea lays out, in plain language, the four federal laws that do most of the work of protecting students online, so that school staff can tell them apart instead of treating privacy as one undifferentiated obligation. FERPA protects student education records, COPPA protects the personal information of children under 13 when they use commercial websites and apps, and CIPA sets rules for internet filtering and safety in schools that receive federal discounts for internet service. The Protection of Pupil Rights Amendment is the fourth, giving parents rights over surveys and marketing that involve their children. It matters less for most AI tools, but it can apply when a tool asks students about sensitive topics. The problem it solves is confusion: each law answers a different question, and a school that cannot say which one is in play cannot tell what it owes students and families.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In day to day school work, the four laws map onto different moments rather than one single review. When a district stores, shares or gives access to student education records, FERPA is the frame, and that includes records that AI tools may generate or hold. When a commercial website or app collects personal information from a child under 13, COPPA is the frame, which shapes what a school can let younger students sign up for. CIPA governs internet filtering and safety for schools that receive federal discounts for internet service, so it sits with the network and filtering decisions rather than with a single lesson. The Protection of Pupil Rights Amendment comes into play when a tool asks students about sensitive topics, because it gives parents rights over surveys and marketing involving their children. The text does not give separate grade band guidance beyond the under 13 line in COPPA.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text presents these four laws as the legal backdrop rather than as findings from a study, and it offers no research label, sample or figure for the idea itself. Its one concrete reference is Figure 3.2, which sets the four laws side by side, and the text says each law gets a closer look in the pages that follow, with attention to how AI changes what they ask of a school. No study, statistic or measured outcome is stated here. On the supplied text alone, this idea rests on the law and on practice rather than on research evidence.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits here are about scope and about who decides. The text notes that the Protection of Pupil Rights Amendment matters less for most AI tools, so it should not be stretched to cover every situation, though it can apply when a tool asks students about sensitive topics. Each law is described as doing part of the work, which means no single one of them covers everything a school does with AI. The text does not set out penalties, deadlines or compliance steps, and it does not say who inside a school makes the final call. Those judgments, and any decision about a specific tool or record, stay with the people responsible for the school and its students, and this page describes practice rather than giving legal advice.
